q: A technician needs to attach an RJ-45 connector to the end of a Cat6 cable. Which tool is required?

q: A technician is terminating Cat6 cable into a keystone jack in a wall plate. Which tool is used to seat each conductor into the jack?
explanation: A punchdown tool (impact tool) pushes individual conductors into the IDC (insulation displacement contact) slots of a keystone jack or patch panel (110-block standard). The blade cuts excess wire flush during the punch.

q: After terminating a patch cable, a technician wants to verify that all eight conductors are connected in the correct order and there are no open pairs. Which tool performs this test?
explanation: A cable tester (continuity tester) verifies that each pin on one end maps correctly to the matching pin on the other end. It detects opens (broken conductors), shorts (conductors touching), reversed pairs, and miswires. It does not measure signal quality or bandwidth.

q: A technician cannot locate which port in the patch panel corresponds to the wall jack in room 204. Which tool pair is used to identify the cable?
explanation: A toner probe has two parts: a tone generator attached to one end of the cable injects an audio signal, and the inductive amplifier (probe) detects the signal by proximity — no electrical contact required. This allows tracing cables through walls, ceilings, and patch panels without cutting into anyt

q: A technician suspects a NIC or switch port is faulty but the network cable and switch appear functional. Which tool tests the port in isolation?
explanation: A loopback plug connects the transmit (TX) pair to the receive (RX) pair on the same port. When the NIC or switch port sends a signal, it receives its own signal back. Diagnostic software confirms whether the port hardware is functioning. This test isolates the port from all external cable and netwo

q: A user reports intermittent Wi-Fi drops. The technician suspects channel interference from neighboring networks. Which tool identifies overlapping channels and signal strength?
explanation: A Wi-Fi analyzer (software or dedicated hardware) displays all visible SSIDs, their broadcast channels, signal strength (dBm), and security type. It identifies channel overlap — a common cause of interference on the 2.4 GHz band where only channels 1, 6, and 11 are non-overlapping.

q: A network administrator needs to capture all traffic passing between a firewall and a core switch without disrupting active connections. Which device accomplishes this passively?
explanation: A network tap (test access point) is an inline passive device that copies all traffic to a monitoring port without affecting the live data flow. Unlike a SPAN port on a switch, a tap cannot drop packets due to oversubscription and does not require switch configuration.

q: Which networking tool is specifically designed to remove the outer jacket of a UTP cable without cutting through the inner conductor insulation?
explanation: A cable stripper (jacket stripper) uses an adjustable blade depth that scores and removes only the outer PVC jacket. q: Which tool would a technician use to verify that a newly installed structured cabling run meets Cat6 performance specifications (attenuation, NEXT, return loss)?
explanation: A cable certifier (e.g., Fluke DSX series) performs full electrical characterization: insertion loss, near-end crosstalk (NEXT), return loss, and propagation delay. It certifies compliance with TIA/EIA standards. A basic continuity tester only checks wiring order — it cannot certify performance spec

q: A technician needs to identify which wall port connects to a specific patch panel port in a wiring closet without labeled cables. Which tool should they use?
explanation: A toner probe sends a tone signal down the cable; the inductive amplifier probe detects it at the other end, allowing the technician to identify cable runs. A cable certifier tests electrical performance specifications, not cable tracing.
